additions.reason: The Rebbe re-reads the Gemara phrase 'נָתַן בּוֹ עֵינָיו' as a bechina of the act of seeing through the Tzaddik's eyes: 'כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רוֹאֶה בְּעֵינֵיהֶם שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים'. The fixing of eyes upon someone by a sage is equated with the act of making the sinner see through the Tzaddik's lens — a positive act of revelation from the Tzaddik's side. The concept belongs in Package 1 as the action-form of the Tzaddik's visionary capacity.

additions.reason: The Rebbe derives 'גַּל' from 'הִתְגַּלּוּת' (revelation): 'גַּל מִלְּשׁוֹן הִתְגַּלּוּת'. This is an explicit linguistic bechina — the word 'heap' (gal) is re-read as 'revelation' (gilui). In this positive reading, the Tzaddik's gaze causes a revelation of the spiritual reality that was previously hidden. This belongs in Package 1 as an aspect of the revealing/illuminating power of the Tzaddik's vision.

additions.node_text: עֲצָמוֹת מִלְּשׁוֹן עוֹצֵם עֵינָיו מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע
additions.reason: The Rebbe derives 'עֲצָמוֹת' (bones) from 'עוֹצֵם עֵינָיו מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע' (one who closes his eyes from seeing evil — Isaiah 33:15). This is an explicit linguistic bechina: עֲצָמוֹת shares its root with עוֹצֵם (closing/shutting eyes). In the context of the sinner, the 'heap of bones' represents the state of willful blindness — the sinner who closes his eyes to the evil he is doing. The punishment ('גַּל שֶׁל עֲצָמוֹת') is precisely the forced opening of those eyes to see what they were shut from seeing. This belongs in Package 2 as the core evil-mirror concept: where the Tzaddik's eyes are open and penetrating (Package 1), the sinner's eyes are shut (עֲצָמוֹת = eye-closing) and concealed from truth.

additions.node_text: גַּל שֶׁל עֲצָמוֹת — רְאִיַּת הַפְּגָם הַנֶּעֶלָם
additions.reason: The complete phrase 'נַעֲשָׂה גַּל שֶׁל עֲצָמוֹת' is decoded as: the sinner sees what he damaged, which had been hidden from him before — 'שֶׁהָיָה נִסְתָּר מִמֶּנּוּ מִקֹּדֶם'. This is the supreme punishment: 'אֵין עֹנֶשׁ גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה, כְּשֶׁאָדָם רוֹאֶה מַה שֶּׁפָּגַם'. The 'heap of bones' is the bechina of forced self-revelation of spiritual destruction. This belongs in Package 2 as the consequence/punishment aspect of sin — the sinner forced to see, in full, through the Tzaddik's eyes, what he has wrought.

analysis_notes.structural_note: Torah #98 is the shortest Torah in LM1 that has been analyzed. Its 5-line structure contains one compressed teaching: the good/evil mirror of seeing versus blindness. The Tzaddik's open, divine eyes (Package 1 / good) are the exact mirror of the sinner's shut eyes (Package 2 / evil = עֲצָמוֹת). Both packages are structured around the same act — seeing — but from opposite poles of the cosmos: God-vision vs. self-blinding. The word גַּל appears in both packages under different readings: as הִתְגַּלּוּת (revelation, good) and as גַּל שֶׁל עֲצָמוֹת (heap of bones = forced revelation of damage, evil). This dual reading of גַּל is itself the hinge-concept of the Torah.
